Caspian Sea.text: Its surface sits about 27 m below sea level, and its water is about a third as salty as seawater.
Caspian Sea.evidence: It has a salinity of approximately 1.2% (12 g/L), about a third of the salinity of average seawater. ... Its gross coverage is 386,400 km2 (149,200 sq mi) and the surface is about 27 m (89 ft) below sea level.

Superior.text: French explorers called it le lac supérieur, the upper lake, because it sits above Lake Huron.
Superior.evidence: In the 17th century, the first French explorers approached the great inland sea by way of the Ottawa River and Lake Huron; they referred to their discovery as le lac supérieur (the upper lake, i.e., above Lake Huron in elevation).

Victoria.text: Renamed after Queen Victoria by John Hanning Speke, the first Briton to document it, in 1858.
Victoria.evidence: Though having multiple local language names (Swahili: Ziwa Nyanza; Dholuo: Nam Lolwe; Luganda: 'Nnalubaale; Kinyarwanda: Nyanza), the lake was renamed after Queen Victoria by the explorer John Hanning Speke, the first Briton to document it in 1858, while on an expedition with Richard Francis Burton.

Huron.text: Contains Manitoulin Island, the largest freshwater island on Earth.
Huron.evidence: A notable feature of the lake is Manitoulin Island, which separates the North Channel and Georgian Bay from the main basin. It is the largest freshwater island on Earth.

Michigan.text: The only Great Lake located fully in the United States.
Michigan.evidence: Lake Michigan is the only Great Lake located fully in the United States; the other four are shared between the U.S. and Canada.

Tanganyika.text: The world's longest freshwater lake, and one of only twenty lakes more than a million years old.
Tanganyika.evidence: It is the world's longest freshwater lake. ... Lake Tanganyika is an ancient lake, one of only twenty more than a million years old.

Baikal.text: Holds more fresh water than all of the North American Great Lakes combined.
Baikal.evidence: However, because it is also the deepest lake, with a maximum depth of 1,642 metres (5,387 feet), Lake Baikal is the world's largest freshwater lake by volume, containing 23,615.39 km3 (5,670 cu mi) of water or 22–23% of the world's fresh surface water, more than all of the North American Great Lakes combined.

Great Bear Lake.text: Explorer John Franklin wrote in 1828 that a white rag in its water stayed visible to 15 fathoms.
Great Bear Lake.evidence: The lake is known for its considerable clarity. Explorer John Franklin wrote in 1828 that a white rag placed in the water did not disappear until it exceeded a depth of 15 fathoms (90 ft; 27 m).

Malawi.text: Home to more fish species than any other lake, including at least 700 species of cichlid.
Malawi.evidence: Lake Malawi is home to more species of fish than any other lake in the world, including at least 700 species of cichlid.

Great Slave Lake.text: North America's deepest lake; a 1930s gold find on its North Arm led to the founding of Yellowknife.
Great Slave Lake.evidence: Great Slave Lake is the second-largest lake in the Northwest Territories, Canada (after Great Bear Lake), the deepest lake in North America at 614 m (2,014 ft), and the tenth-largest lake in the world by area. ... In the 1930s, gold was discovered on the North Arm of Great Slave Lake. This discovery led to the establishment of Yellowknife, which would become the capital of the NWT.
